title: Interview or interrogation?
header_line: My analysis of one book on an entrepreneur's life. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: Do you interview, or do you interrogate?

I said that there are two different ways to extract information from people: an interview, which is free-flowing, relaxed discussion; and an interrogation. Interrogation is a scary word, but it is basically a persuasive method to get somebody to tell the truth in a controlled environment.

A student said: the approach was really direct, question after question. There could be a lot of bias in that, if you are only asking yes or no questions. You may be trying to justify an answer you've already come to.

Another said: I like the conversational approach. The more relaxed you make them, the better the interview, because you get a truer sense of who they are. Most people get nervous in interviews, and you might miss a good candidate. Yes or no questions sound like confirmation bias: trying to confirm what you already think.

I said: when he goes down the manufacturing line, I don't think he is free-flowing. I see him in a very open-and-closed question scenario. A student said: it is a very objective outlook on right and wrong, black and white, but he lives in the gray.

A student said the ten-people question may be statistical: if you are really someone who can be trusted with highly sensitive information, you naturally have to be biased toward not trusting people, so you wouldn't rattle off ten.

I said: the learning lesson here is: what is our particular style? Are we free-flowing, making people feel comfortable? Or more interrogative? Maybe there is something to be learned about balancing the two. There are times to be free-flowing, compassionate, empathetic, and times to be more black and white, objective and factual.

A student said: there are times when he is looking for fresh information and times when he is validating a pre-existing disposition, but his level of intensity makes it all feel like an interrogation.
Which style would your last three conversations have been?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write your style: free-flowing or interrogative.
Write how you avoid confirmation bias in your questions.
Write what you would ask differently to relax a nervous candidate.
Write how you would balance the two.

check.q: How did I describe an interrogation?
choices: A persuasive method to get somebody to tell the truth in a controlled environment

check.q: What did a student warn yes or no questions can lead to?
What did I say about style?
choices: Maybe balance the two: free-flowing and interrogative

recap: Know whether you interview or interrogate. Avoid confirmation bias. Balance the two.
